purpose: systems feasibility only, not a model benchmark -- no model-quality claim should be read from this file
correction_note: That profile (commit 9b65b33) correctly identified the encoder's per-relation message-passing loop as the real memory driver, and commit a998448 added per-layer gradient checkpointing, which measurably helped (~25-28% peak memory reduction at every subset size) but did not fix feasibility (still OOM at 4M triples). The natural next hypothesis was that checkpointing needed to be finer-grained -- per relation, not per layer, since a single per-layer recompute-then-backward call still needed every one of that layer's 66 relations' gathered input slices alive simultaneously. Commit d555789 implemented exactly that. This profile shows that hypothesis was ALSO wrong: per-relation checkpointing measured WORSE than per-layer checkpointing (6324.5 MB vs 5275.7 MB peak at 1,000,000 triples -- a regression, not an improvement), and still OOM'd at 4,000,000 triples, identically to every prior configuration. Per-relation checkpointing has been reverted (git revert of d555789, restoring a998448's per-layer approach, the best-measured configuration found so far) rather than kept as a regression.

feasibility_decision.reason: every configuration tested (no checkpointing, per-layer checkpointing, per-relation checkpointing) OOMs at 4,000,000 triples -- less than half the full 8,097,798-triple tuning set -- on a 14.6 GB T4
feasibility_decision.best_configuration_found: per-layer gradient checkpointing (commit a998448 / current HEAD 80c34a9), ~25-28% peak memory reduction vs. no checkpointing, still insufficient for full scale

next_step_note: Stopping further speculative architecture changes here. Three real-GPU-measured attempts (gradient accumulation alone: no memory effect, correct but not the bottleneck; per-layer checkpointing: best result, ~28% reduction, insufficient; per-relation checkpointing: worse than per-layer, reverted) indicate the current understanding of where this encoder's memory actually goes is incomplete -- reasoning from first principles has now twice produced a wrong prediction. Continuing to guess at architectural changes without better diagnostic tooling (e.g. torch.cuda.memory._record_memory_history / a real memory snapshot at the peak moment) is not a productive use of further Kaggle GPU time. Recommended next step is either (a) an actual memory-profiling pass to see what is allocated at the peak moment, before any further architecture change, or (b) a explicit methodological decision (smaller hidden_dim/fewer bases, real neighbor sampling, subgraph mini-batching, graph partitioning, or more GPU memory) -- the user's call, not an autonomous one.
